query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dominant mechanism governing wear performance in high‐entropy alloy protective coatings is the in situ formation of a continuous, protective oxide/spinel layer at the surface. Increasing the ambient oxygen partial pressure during wear leads to a more refined and robust protective layer that reduces friction and material loss during sliding contact.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy protective coating with a multicomponent microstructure deposited under conventional conditions, exhibiting a baseline oxide layer developed under ambient air (21% O2).
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the ambient oxygen partial pressure during wear testing (or conversely reduce it in a separate trial) to control the formation, thickness, and continuity of the protective oxide/spinel layer.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted under reciprocating sliding or similar contact conditions at elevated temperatures (e.g., conditions mimicking real-world wear in moderate-to-high thermal environments) where oxidation kinetics are appreciable.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and evolution of a continuous oxide/spinel layer at the coating surface and critical grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced oxygen availability promotes the formation of a protective, adherent oxide/spinel layer that acts as a barrier against abrasive wear. This layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, thus lowering friction coefficients and wear depth.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under increased oxygen partial pressures, the oxide/spinel layer will be thicker and more continuous, leading to a measurable reduction in wear rate (lower material loss and friction coefficient) compared to the baseline established in ambient air. Conversely, lowering the oxygen partial pressure should yield a less protective oxide layer and higher wear rates.
generation.baseline: Wear performance measured in standard ambient air (with 21% oxygen) where the oxide/spinel layer forms naturally without controlled modification.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold over the range of oxygen partial pressures and temperatures at which oxidation kinetics are active (typically at elevated temperatures used in wear testing). Extreme conditions (e.g., very low temperatures or pressures where oxidation is negligible) are outside the scope of this hypothesis.
generation.uncertainty: While prior observations correlate protective oxide formation with improved wear resistance, the quantitative relationship between oxygen partial pressure, oxide layer properties, and wear performance is not yet well established and may be influenced by alloy composition and testing temperature.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of wear tests on identical HEA coatings under controlled oxygen partial pressures. One set of tests should be run in standard ambient air (baseline) and another in an elevated oxygen environment. A third set, where oxygen is minimized (via inert gas atmosphere), will serve as a negative control. Simultaneously monitor the evolution of the oxide/spinel layer using in situ surface analysis (e.g., high-temperature XRD or electron microscopy) and record wear rates and friction coefficients.
measurements: Thickness and continuity of the oxide/spinel layer
Wear rate (mass loss or wear track depth)
Surface morphology and microstructural characterization post-test
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If systematic modification of the ambient oxygen partial pressure does not lead to a directional change in oxide/spinel layer formation (i.e., no improvement in layer continuity) or if no corresponding change (reduction) in wear performance is observed compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis that the protective oxide/spinel layer is the dominant mechanism governing wear performance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. frame.goal: To elucidate a single mechanistic process that governs the wear performance of HEA coatings by linking microstructural features (such as phase stability, grain boundaries, and oxidation layers) to observed wear resistance.
frame.limitation: The current understanding lacks a clear, testable mechanistic framework that isolates the dominant factor responsible for wear behavior in HEA coatings.

decision.trend: Research on HEA wear behavior has evolved from separately noting benefits from microstructural factors such as grain refinement, phase stability, and the incidental formation of oxide or spinel phases to recognizing that the in situ formation of a protective surface layer during high-temperature wear testing can reduce friction and wear depth. In studies like PMC7515071, increased wear resistance at elevated temperatures was linked to the appearance of a spinel phase, suggesting that changes in microstructure under load and temperature provide a barrier mechanism. However, these works did not isolate a single controlled variable to definitively identify the mechanistic role of such protective layers in governing wear performance.
decision.unsolved: There remains no single, testable hypothesis that explicitly ties the formation or modification of a controllable microstructural feature—such as a protective oxide or spinel layer at critical grain boundaries—to the observed improvement in wear resistance. The challenge is to distinguish whether the improvement arises primarily from the oxide layer evolution or from other concurrent microstructural changes.
decision.lever: Systematically adjust the ambient oxygen partial pressure during wear testing to control the formation, thickness, and continuity of the protective oxide/spinel layer on the HEA coating
decision.why: This lever follows from the trend where improved wear resistance correlates with protective phase formation. By controlling oxygen availability, the experiment directly tests whether refining the oxide layer (compared to a baseline run in standard air) leads to a directional change in wear performance. This approach isolates a single mechanism and sets clear observational criteria (improved resistance when the oxide layer is enhanced) and a falsification scenario (no change or adverse wear behavior despite controlled oxidation).
